title: Google Escapes Ad Tech Breakup as Judge Rejects DOJ Forced Sale
excerpt: Federal judge opts for behavioral remedies over structural separation, marking the third consecutive failure by U.S. antitrust enforcers to break up a major tech company.
body:
• U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema rejected the Justice Department's bid to force Google to sell its AdX advertising exchange, opting for behavioral remedies instead
  • The ruling marks the third consecutive time a federal judge has denied government efforts to break up a major tech company, following failed attempts with Meta and Google's Chrome browser
  • Google must make its ad tech tools interoperable with rival platforms, with both parties required to submit a joint final judgment proposal within 30 days
  • Alphabet shares rose about 1% to $338.51 following the decision, while Google announced plans to appeal the underlying monopoly finding from April 2025

Judge Chooses Restraint Over Breakup

A federal judge on Wednesday declined to break up Google's advertising technology business, rejecting the Justice Department's push for a forced sale of the company's online ad exchange in what amounts to a landmark defeat for U.S. antitrust enforcement against Big Tech.

U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema in Alexandria, Virginia, sided with Google in the remedies phase of the case, opting for behavioral changes rather than the structural separation prosecutors had demanded. In a two-page order, Brinkema accepted most of the parties' proposed behavioral remedies, requiring Google to make its ad tech stack interoperable with rival platforms.

The DOJ had argued that Google could not be trusted to operate AdX — the real-time auction platform where publishers pay a 20% fee to sell advertising space — given the company's history of anticompetitive conduct. Prosecutors compared Google's integrated position to owning the New York Stock Exchange while simultaneously being its biggest buyer and seller.

"We're very pleased the court rejected the DOJ's proposal to break apart tools that help small businesses reach new customers and grow."

— Lee-Anne Mulholland, Google Vice President of Regulatory Affairs

Background: The Monopoly Finding

The case dates to 2023, when the DOJ and a broad coalition of states sued Google over its dominance in advertising technology markets. In April 2025, Brinkema ruled that Google holds illegal monopolies on servers that host publisher ads and on ad exchanges that sit between buyers and sellers, finding that the company unlawfully locked publishers into using its AdX platform.

Google's advertising revenue reached approximately $294 billion in 2025, with the ad tech division representing roughly 12% of Alphabet's total revenue. Ad Manager specifically accounted for 4.1% of Google's overall revenue and 1.5% of operating profit in 2020, according to Wedbush research.

Google plans to appeal the underlying April 2025 liability ruling, adding uncertainty about whether the interoperability requirements will ultimately take effect.

A Pattern of Failed Breakup Attempts

Wednesday's decision is the third consecutive time a federal judge has rejected government efforts to break up a major technology company — a pattern that raises questions about whether antitrust law can effectively check Big Tech's market power.

Last year, a federal judge in Washington rejected the Federal Trade Commission's attempt to force Meta Platforms to sell Instagram and WhatsApp, ruling that the agency failed to prove Meta holds a monopoly in social media. Separately, another Washington judge who had found Google holds an illegal monopoly in online search rejected the DOJ's bid to force a Chrome browser sale, citing rising competition from generative AI companies like OpenAI.

Pending antitrust cases against Amazon and Apple involving smartphone and online retail markets are not expected to reach trial until 2027 at the earliest.

What Comes Next

Both Google and the DOJ must submit a joint final judgment proposal within 30 days. The full redacted decision will be released later this month after a 14-day period to allow for confidentiality redactions.

The DOJ said it was "pleased that the court ordered substantial relief" and that it is "evaluating appropriate next steps," leaving open the possibility of an appeal. Alphabet stock advanced about 1% to $338.51 on Wednesday.
nri_angle: The ruling affects the broader tech industry where many Indian-origin professionals work, and has implications for digital advertising costs that impact Indian-American small business owners.
